He has no systemic infectious signs and a negative respiratory viral panel. Flexible laryngoscopy and operative microlaryngoscopy/bronchoscopy showed a normal airway, arguing against fixed structural lesions (subglottic stenosis, tracheal foreign body, vocal fold paralysis) and against acute infectious/edematous processes that would be visible. The cough/stridor began immediately post‑op and was refractory to bronchodilator, benzodiazepine, inhaled steroid and antitussive therapies. The case includes an illustration of the auricular branch of the vagus (Arnold) nerve, directing attention to ear‑canal/middle‑ear vagal stimulation. The auricular branch (Arnold) reflex is a known cause of an otogenic cough and can provoke vigorous coughing or laryngospasm/stridor when stimulated (e.g., by ear canal or middle ear irritation after otologic procedures). Intermittent paradoxical vocal fold motion (vocal cord dysfunction) can present with noisy breathing and normal airway exam if not captured during an episode. Post‑intubation/subglottic edema or transient laryngospasm from airway irritation are possible but would usually be seen on airway exam or be more transient. Psychogenic (habit) cough is unlikely because it typically abates during sleep. Putting these data together, the most likely diagnosis is an otogenic cough mediated by the auricular branch (Arnold) reflex triggered by the recent ear surgery; other plausible differentials (in order) are paradoxical vocal fold motion, postoperative laryngeal hypersensitivity/irritation (including reflux‑provoked laryngospasm), transient post‑intubation/subglottic edema, and (least likely) psychogenic/habit cough.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Otogenic cough due to stimulation of the auricular branch of the vagus (Arnold reflex) after tympanostomy/adenoid surgery (most likely)
2. Paradoxical vocal fold motion (vocal cord dysfunction) — intermittent glottic adduction not captured on scope
3. Postoperative laryngeal hypersensitivity / recurrent laryngospasm from airway irritation or laryngopharyngeal reflux
4. Transient post‑intubation/subglottic edema or mucosal irritation causing biphasic stridor
5. Psychogenic (habit) cough (least likely given persistence during sleep)
